title: Genre-specific section requirements of the corpus templates (PEP 1/12, Rust RFC, KEP, Go design doc, RFC 7322, RFC 3552, Oxide RFD 1, Shape Up)

criteria.name: Start with an idea for Python

definition.text: It is highly recommended that a single PEP contain a single key proposal or new idea; the more focused the PEP, the more successful it tends to be.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'Start with an idea for Python'

criteria.name: PEP Review & Resolution (minimum criteria)

definition.text: For a PEP to be accepted it must meet certain minimum criteria. It must be a clear and complete description of the proposed enhancement. The enhancement must represent a net improvement. The proposed implementation, if applicable, must be solid and must not complicate the interpreter unduly.

criteria.condition: The proposed implementation, if applicable

definition.text: Preamble -- :rfc:`2822` style headers containing meta-data about the PEP, including the PEP number, a short descriptive title (limited to a maximum of 44 characters), the names, and optionally the contact info for each author, etc.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 1

definition.text: Abstract -- a short (~200 word) description of the technical issue being addressed.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 2

criteria.name: Motivation

definition.text: Motivation -- The motivation is critical for PEPs that want to change the Python language, library, or ecosystem. It should clearly explain why the existing language specification is inadequate to address the problem that the PEP solves. … PEP submissions without sufficient motivation may be rejected.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 3

criteria.condition: for PEPs that want to change the Python language, library, or ecosystem

definition.text: Specification -- The technical specification should describe the syntax and semantics of any new language feature. The specification should be detailed enough to allow competing, interoperable implementations for at least the current major Python platforms (CPython, Jython, IronPython, PyPy).
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 4

definition.text: Rationale -- The rationale fleshes out the specification by describing why particular design decisions were made. It should describe alternate designs that were considered and related work, e.g. how the feature is supported in other languages. The rationale should provide evidence of consensus within the community and discuss important objections or concerns raised during discussion.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 5

criteria.name: Backwards Compatibility

definition.text: Backwards Compatibility -- All PEPs that introduce backwards incompatibilities must include a section describing these incompatibilities and their severity. The PEP must explain how the author proposes to deal with these incompatibilities. PEP submissions without a sufficient backwards compatibility treatise may be rejected outright.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 6

criteria.condition: All PEPs that introduce backwards incompatibilities

criteria.name: Security Implications

definition.text: Security Implications -- If there are security concerns in relation to the PEP, those concerns should be explicitly written out to make sure reviewers of the PEP are aware of them.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 7

criteria.condition: If there are security concerns in relation to the PEP

criteria.name: How to Teach This

definition.text: How to Teach This -- For a PEP that adds new functionality or changes language behavior, it is helpful to include a section on how to teach users, new and experienced, how to apply the PEP to their work.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 8

criteria.condition: For a PEP that adds new functionality or changes language behavior

criteria.name: Reference Implementation

definition.text: The final implementation must include test code and documentation appropriate for either the Python language reference or the standard library reference.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 9

criteria.condition: The reference implementation must be completed before any PEP is given status "Final", but it need not be completed before the PEP is accepted.

definition.text: Rejected Ideas -- Throughout the discussion of a PEP, various ideas will be proposed which are not accepted. Those rejected ideas should be recorded along with the reasoning as to why they were rejected.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 10

criteria.name: Open Issues

definition.text: Open Issues -- While a PEP is in draft, ideas can come up which warrant further discussion. Those ideas should be recorded so people know that they are being thought about but do not have a concrete resolution.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 11

criteria.condition: While a PEP is in draft

definition.text: Acknowledgements -- Useful to thank and acknowledge people who have helped develop, discuss, or draft the PEP, or for any other purpose.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 12

definition.text: Footnotes -- A collection of footnotes cited in the PEP, and a place to list non-inline hyperlink targets.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 13

criteria.name: Change History

definition.text: Change History -- A summary of major changes the PEP has undergone, based on discussions and feedback.
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 14

criteria.condition: This isn't mandatory, so it's left to the PEP author's discretion

definition.text: Copyright/license -- Each new PEP must be placed under a dual license of public domain and CC0-1.0-Universal_
definition.locator: PEP 1, 'What belongs in a successful PEP?', item 15

definition.text: One paragraph explanation of the feature.

Any changes to Rust should focus on solving a problem that users of Rust are having. This section should explain this problem in detail, including necessary background. It should also contain several specific use cases where this feature can help a user, and explain how it helps.

criteria.name: Guide-level explanation

definition.text: Explain the proposal as if it was already included in the language and you were teaching it to another Rust programmer. That generally means: - Introducing new named concepts. - Explaining the feature largely in terms of examples. - Explaining how Rust programmers should think about the feature, and how it should impact the way they use Rust. It should explain the impact as concretely as possible.

criteria.condition: For implementation-oriented RFCs (e.g. for compiler internals), this section should focus on how compiler contributors should think about the change, and give examples of its concrete impact. For policy RFCs, this section should provide an example-driven introduction to the policy, and explain its impact in concrete terms.

definition.text: This is the technical portion of the RFC. Explain the design in sufficient detail that: - Its interaction with other features is clear. - It is reasonably clear how the feature would be implemented. - Corner cases are dissected by example. The section should return to the examples given in the previous section, and explain more fully how the detailed proposal makes those examples work.
Why should we not do this?
- Why is this design the best in the space of possible designs? - What other designs have been considered and what is the rationale for not choosing them? - What is the impact of not doing this?
definition.locator: Rust RFC template (0000-template.md), section 'Rationale and alternatives'

criteria.name: Rationale and alternatives

definition.text: If this is a language proposal, could this be done in a library or macro instead? Does the proposed change make Rust code easier or harder to read, understand, and maintain?
definition.locator: Rust RFC template (0000-template.md), section 'Rationale and alternatives'

criteria.condition: If this is a language proposal

criteria.name: Prior art

definition.text: Discuss prior art, both the good and the bad, in relation to this proposal.

criteria.condition: If there is no prior art, that is fine - your ideas are interesting to us whether they are brand new or if it is an adaptation from other languages.

definition.text: - What parts of the design do you expect to resolve through the RFC process before this gets merged? - What parts of the design do you expect to resolve through the implementation of this feature before stabilization? - What related issues do you consider out of scope for this RFC that could be addressed in the future independently of the solution that comes out of this RFC?

criteria.name: Future possibilities

definition.text: Think about what the natural extension and evolution of your proposal would be and how it would affect the language and project as a whole in a holistic way.

criteria.condition: If you have tried and cannot think of any future possibilities, you may simply state that you cannot think of anything.

criteria.name: Fill out this file as best you can.

definition.text: At minimum, you should fill in the "Summary" and "Motivation" sections.

criteria.condition: Avoid getting hung up on specific details and instead aim to get the goals of the KEP clarified and merged quickly. The best way to do this is to just start with the high-level sections and fill out details incrementally in subsequent PRs.

criteria.name: UNRESOLVED

definition.text: Any KEP marked as `provisional` is a working document and subject to change. You can denote sections that are under active debate as follows:

criteria.condition: Any KEP marked as `provisional`

definition.text: This section is incredibly important for producing high-quality, user-focused documentation such as release notes or a development roadmap. … A good summary is probably at least a paragraph in length.
This section is for explicitly listing the motivation, goals, and non-goals of this KEP. Describe why the change is important and the benefits to users.
List the specific goals of the KEP. What is it trying to achieve? How will we know that this has succeeded?
What is out of scope for this KEP? Listing non-goals helps to focus discussion and make progress.

This is where we get down to the specifics of what the proposal actually is. This should have enough detail that reviewers can understand exactly what you're proposing, but should not include things like API designs or implementation. What is the desired outcome and how do we measure success?.

criteria.name: User Stories (Optional)

definition.text: Detail the things that people will be able to do if this KEP is implemented. Include as much detail as possible so that people can understand the "how" of the system. The goal here is to make this feel real for users without getting bogged down.

criteria.condition: (Optional)

criteria.name: Notes/Constraints/Caveats (Optional)

definition.text: What are the caveats to the proposal? What are some important details that didn't come across above? Go in to as much detail as necessary here.

criteria.condition: (Optional)

definition.text: What are the risks of this proposal, and how do we mitigate? Think broadly. For example, consider both security and how this will impact the larger Kubernetes ecosystem. How will security be reviewed, and by whom? How will UX be reviewed, and by whom?

This section should contain enough information that the specifics of your change are understandable. This may include API specs (though not always required) or even code snippets. If there's any ambiguity about HOW your proposal will be implemented, this is the place to discuss them.

criteria.name: Test Plan

definition.text: The goal is to ensure that we don't accept enhancements with inadequate testing. All code is expected to have adequate tests (eventually with coverage expectations).

criteria.condition: Not required until targeted at a release.

criteria.name: Prerequisite testing updates

definition.text: Based on reviewers feedback describe what additional tests need to be added prior implementing this enhancement to ensure the enhancements have also solid foundations.

criteria.condition: Not required until targeted at a release.

criteria.name: Unit tests

definition.text: In principle every added code should have complete unit test coverage, so providing the exact set of tests will not bring additional value. However, if complete unit test coverage is not possible, explain the reason of it together with explanation why this is acceptable.

criteria.condition: Not required until targeted at a release.

criteria.name: Integration tests

definition.text: For Alpha, describe what tests will be added to ensure proper quality of the enhancement. For Beta and GA, document that tests have been written, have been executed regularly, and have been stable.

definition.text: Production readiness reviews are intended to ensure that features merging into Kubernetes are observable, scalable and supportable; can be safely operated in production environments, and can be disabled or rolled back in the event they cause increased failures in production.

definition.text: The design doc should address any specific concerns raised during the initial discussion.

criteria.name: Language changes

definition.text: As explained in the blog entry, language change proposals should - address an important issue for many people, - have minimal impact on everybody else, and - come with a clear and well-understood solution.

criteria.condition: language change proposals

criteria.name: RFC Editor's Philosophy

definition.text: Make the document as clear, consistent, and readable as possible. - Correct larger content/clarity issues; flag any unclear passages for author review. - Fix inconsistencies (e.g., terms that appear in various forms, text that appears multiple times, or inconsistent capitalization).

criteria.condition: If the original wording is a more accurate representation of the technical content being described in the document, it takes precedence over editorial conventions.

definition.text: The RFC publication language is English. Spelling may be either American or British, as long as an individual document is internally consistent.

No overstriking (or underlining) is allowed. * When a sentence ended by a period is immediately followed by another sentence, there must be two blank spaces after the period. * A comma is used before the last item of a series
DNS names, whether or not in URIs, that are used as generic examples in RFCs should use the particular examples defined in "Reserved Top Level DNS Names" [BCP32], to avoid accidental conflicts.
Capitalization must be consistent within the document and ideally should be consistent with related RFCs.
References and citations must match. That is, there must be a reference for each citation used, and vice versa.

criteria.name: Abbreviation Rules

definition.text: Abbreviations should be expanded in document titles and upon first use in the document. The full expansion of the text should be followed by the abbreviation itself in parentheses.

criteria.condition: The exception is an abbreviation that is so common that the readership of RFCs can be expected to recognize it immediately; examples include (but are not limited to) TCP, IP, SNMP, and HTTP.

definition.text: Within the body of the memo, the order shown above is strongly recommended. Exceptions may be questioned. Outside the body of the memo, the order above is required.
Choosing a good title for an RFC can be a challenge. A good title should fairly represent the scope and purpose of the document without being either too general or too specific and lengthy.

Every RFC must have an Abstract that provides a concise and comprehensive overview of the purpose and contents of the entire document, to give a technically knowledgeable reader a general overview of the function of the document.

Note also that an Abstract is not a substitute for an Introduction; the RFC should be self-contained as if there were no Abstract. Similarly, the Abstract should be complete in itself. It will appear in isolation in publication announcements and in the online index of RFCs. Therefore, the Abstract must not contain citations.
A Table of Contents (TOC) is required in all RFCs. It must be positioned after the Copyright Notice and before the Introduction.

criteria.name: Body of the Memo

definition.text: Each RFC must include an Introduction section that (among other things) explains the motivation for the RFC and (if appropriate) describes the applicability of the document

criteria.condition: (if appropriate)

definition.text: The body of the memo and the Abstract must be self-contained and separable. This may result in some duplication of text between the Abstract and the Introduction; this is acceptable.

criteria.name: Introduction Section

definition.text: The Introduction section should always be the first section following the TOC (except in the case of MIB module documents).

criteria.condition: (except in the case of MIB module documents)

criteria.condition: Some documents use certain capitalized words ("MUST", "SHOULD", etc.) to specify precise requirement levels for technical features.

criteria.name: IANA Considerations Section

definition.text: It is helpful for authors to clearly identify where text should be updated to reflect the newly assigned values. For example, the use of "TBD1", "TBD2", etc., is recommended in the IANA Considerations section and in the body of the memo.

criteria.condition: The RFC Editor will remove an IANA Considerations section that says there are no IANA considerations (although such a section is required in the Internet-Draft preceding the RFC).

criteria.name: Internationalization Considerations Section

definition.text: All RFCs that deal with internationalization issues should have a section describing those issues

criteria.condition: All RFCs that deal with internationalization issues

definition.text: All RFCs must contain a section that discusses the security considerations relevant to the specification; see "Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations" [BCP72] for more information.

Reference lists must indicate whether each reference is normative or informative, where normative references are essential to implementing or understanding the content of the RFC and informative references provide additional information.

The reference list is solely for recording reference entries. Introductory text is not allowed. The RFC style allows the use of any of a variety of reference styles, as long as they are used consistently within a document.

criteria.name: Acknowledgements Section

definition.text: This optional section may be used instead of, or in addition to, a Contributors section. It is often used by authors to publicly thank those who have provided feedback regarding a document and to note any documents from which text was borrowed.

criteria.condition: This optional section

criteria.name: Contributors Section

definition.text: This optional section acknowledges those who have made significant contributions to the document.

criteria.condition: This optional section

definition.text: This required section gives contact information for the author(s) listed in the first-page header. Contact information must include a long-lived email address and optionally may include a postal address and/or telephone number.

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: There should be a clear description of the kinds of threats on the described protocol or technology. This should be approached as an effort to perform "due diligence" in describing all known or foreseeable risks and threats to potential implementers and users.

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: Authors MUST describe 1. which attacks are out of scope (and why!) 2. which attacks are in-scope 2.1 and the protocol is susceptible to 2.2 and the protocol protects against

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: At least the following forms of attack MUST be considered: eavesdropping, replay, message insertion, deletion, modification, and man-in-the-middle. Potential denial of service attacks MUST be identified as well.

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: it should be clearly indicated which portions of the data are protected and what the protections are (i.e., integrity only, confidentiality, and/or endpoint authentication, etc.). Some indication should also be given to what sorts of attacks the cryptographic protection is susceptible. Data which should be held secret (keying material, random seeds, etc.) should be clearly labeled.

criteria.condition: If the protocol incorporates cryptographic protection mechanisms
criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: the security of the authentication method MUST be clearly specified. That is, authors MUST document the assumptions that the security of this authentication method is predicated upon.

criteria.condition: If the technology involves authentication, particularly user-host authentication
criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: It is insufficient to simply state that one's protocol should be run over some lower layer security protocol. If a system relies upon lower layer security services for security, the protections those … services are expected to provide MUST be clearly specified. In addition, the resultant properties of the combined system need to be specified.

criteria.condition: If a system relies upon lower layer security services for security
criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: The threat environment addressed by the Security Considerations section MUST at a minimum include deployment across the global Internet across multiple administrative boundaries without assuming that firewalls are in place, even if only to provide justification for why such consideration is out of scope for the protocol.

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: There should be a clear description of the residual risk to the user or operator of that protocol after threat mitigation has been deployed.

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Writing Security Considerations Sections

definition.text: There should also be some discussion of potential security risks arising from potential misapplications of the protocol or technology described in the RFC.

criteria.document_kind: Security Considerations section of an RFC

criteria.name: Requests for Discussion (RFC 3 spirit)

definition.text: Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples or other specifics, specific suggestions or implementation techniques without introductory or background explication, and explicit questions without any attempted answers are all acceptable.

criteria.condition: Depending on their state, RFDs may be quickly iterated on in a branch, discussed actively as part of a pull request to be merged, or commented upon after having been published.

criteria.name: Insights to include in RFDs

definition.text: Document the viable options (or a subset of options if we can easily rule some out) and the benefits and drawbacks of each option.
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs'

criteria.condition: When writing RFDs for technical and core product determination

criteria.name: Insights to include in RFDs

definition.text: Document our reasoning including data and references wherever possible; making it easy for our future selves (and those who join in the future) to understand the decisions we’ve made and why.
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs'

criteria.condition: When writing RFDs for technical and core product determination

criteria.name: Insights to include in RFDs

definition.text: Document the determination, see [rfd5] for a definition of determination.
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs'

criteria.condition: When writing RFDs for technical and core product determination

criteria.name: Economic

definition.text: What is the relative cost of this idea (and/or alternative ideas) in terms of time and money? … What are the implications that this will have on the company over time, both short-term and long-term?
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs' > business and customer considerations

criteria.condition: While not applicable in every case

criteria.name: Customer outcomes and impact

definition.text: What does this idea look like in terms of how it impacts a customer? … What are the outcomes for customers if we implement this idea versus alternatives?
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs' > business and customer considerations

criteria.condition: While not applicable in every case

definition.text: How do the trade-offs of this determination impact performace? Is it visible to customers? Is it a regression? Are there any benchmarks that helped lead to the determination?
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs' > business and customer considerations

criteria.name: Security

definition.text: How to the trade-offs of this determination impact the security of the product?
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs' > business and customer considerations

definition.text: Not every RFD is equal. Some have more sense of urgency and therefore might not be as rigorous as others. Some are a documentation of our knowledge thus far on a given topic. All things being said, use your best judgement when it comes to the level of depth to devote to an RFD.
definition.locator: Oxide RFD 1, 'Insights to include in RFDs'

definition.text: At the start of every RFD document, we’d like to include a brief amount of metadata.

criteria.name: RFD Metadata and State (ideation)

definition.text: A document in the ideation state contains only a description of the topic that the RFD will cover, providing an indication of the scope of the eventual RFD. … It is critical that RFDs in the ideation state are clear and narrowly defined.

criteria.condition: RFDs in the ideation state

definition.text: There are five ingredients that we always want to include in a pitch:
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 6 'Write the Pitch', introduction

criteria.name: Ingredient 1. Problem

definition.text: Problem — The raw idea, a use case, or something we’ve seen that motivates us to work on this … It’s critical to always present both a problem and a solution together. … The best problem definition consists of a single specific story that shows why the status quo doesn’t work.

criteria.condition: How far you have to go to spell out the problem will depend on how much context you share with the people reading the write-up.

definition.text: Appetite — How much time we want to spend and how that constrains the solution … Stating the appetite in the pitch prevents unproductive conversations.
Solution — The core elements we came up with, presented in a form that’s easy for people to immediately understand … A problem without a solution is unshaped work.

We need to stay high level, but add a little more concreteness than when we worked alone or with a partner. People who read the pitch and look at the drawings without much context need to “get” the idea. We need more concreteness, but we don’t want to over-specify the design with wireframes or high-fidelity mocks.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 6, 'Help them see it'

definition.text: Rabbit holes — Details about the solution worth calling out to avoid problems … Sometimes addressing a rabbit hole just requires a few lines of text.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 6, ingredient list and 'Ingredient 4. Rabbit holes'

definition.text: No-gos — Anything specifically excluded from the concept: functionality or use cases we intentionally aren’t covering to fit the appetite or make the problem tractable … Lastly if there’s anything we’re not doing in this concept, it’s good to mention it here.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 6, ingredient list and 'Ingredient 5. No Gos'

definition.text: When we shape the work, we need to do it at the right level of abstraction: not too vague and not too concrete.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 2 'Principles of Shaping', introduction

definition.text: When design leaders go straight to wireframes or high-fidelity mockups, they define too much detail too early. This leaves designers no room for creativity.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 2, 'Wireframes are too concrete'

definition.text: On the other end of the spectrum, projects that are too vague don’t work either. When a project is defined in a few words, nobody knows what it means. … Team members don’t have enough information to make trade-offs. They don’t know what to include or leave out.
definition.locator: Shape Up ch. 2, 'Words are too abstract'

definition.text: Work in the shaping stage is rough. Everyone can tell by looking at it that it’s unfinished. They can see the open spaces where their contributions will go. Work that’s too fine, too early commits everyone to the wrong details.

Despite being rough and unfinished, shaped work has been thought through. All the main elements of the solution are there at the macro level and they connect together. The work isn’t specified down to individual tasks, but the overall solution is spelled out. … Any open questions or rabbit holes we could see up front have been removed to reduce the project’s risk.
Lastly, shaped work indicates what not to do. It tells the team where to stop. There’s a specific appetite—the amount of time the team is allowed to spend on the project.
